utterances.text: I was in charge of the withdrawal from Sibenik. I secured the withdrawal. I provided the vehicles, the troops. It started on the 25th of September, and lasted until the 25th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During that time, during that period, did this cease-fire hold? Was it breached and was it frequently breached and by whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that on the direction of our withdrawal, violations were less frequent but we had cease-fire violations in the direction of Sinj, and we had cease-fire violations in the direction from the bridge of Sibenik along the direction through Popovici and Kistanje. There were groups infiltrated. They would mine the roads and we had a number of casualties, fatalities of JNA troops and we had some equipment destroyed there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, what were the orders, if there were orders, received by the 9th Corps members from superior commands in terms of population, houses and particularly religious buildings in the area of responsibility of the 9th Corps? Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Orders we received at corps level and the orders issued by the 9th Corps to the subordinated units such as brigades, strictly forbade any destruction, gutting or looting, both of socially owned property and private property of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to bring on to the screens Exhibit 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for Exhibit 26, were such orders complied with, sir? You said orders were received at corps level and the orders issued by the 9th Corps to the subordinated units such as brigades strictly forbade any destruction, gutting or looting. My question is, were such orders complied with, to your knowledge, to the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the unit that I commanded over, these orders were implemented to the letter. There were individual incidents, but these incidents of misconduct by JNA members were sanctioned through courts martial. We had an investigating judge and a Prosecutor at the corps level and all cases of criminal offences or breaches of law we sanctioned those by initiating criminal complaints on the part of commanders. I was one of them. Investigating judges would receive such, prosecute, and process such cases. If you would like me to give you an example, at Drnis, I had a reserve lieutenant, I remembered his name because of his conduct. His name was Baljak Pero, from the village of Zagrovic near Knin. Before the war he used to work in Skopje, Macedonia, and when the call-up orders were issued he heeded the call and he in Drnis raped a woman, a Serb, in front of her underage daughter. He was court martialed at Banja Luka military court. We had other cases. I can only say in connection with this that on the basis of an analysis that I ordered and which is in the records, carried out at the corps level in 1991, on the 23rd of October of 1991, members of the units and the commanders of the JNA of the 9th Corps, in the period of new years eve to October initiated 537 criminal complaints -- I correct myself, 337 criminal complaints against 360 persons. Investigation was carried out against 160. 22 indictments were issued before a court and, at that time, they were processed at the military court at Banja Luka. The Split military court was -- had jurisdiction but because of the blockade of Split we could not process such cases, refer them to Split or send perpetrators, suspects, indicted people, so we had to refer those cases to the Banja Luka military court. Later, at the end of 1991, when the 9th Corps became part of the 2nd Military District, we came under the jurisdiction of the Banja Luka military court. The Banja Luka military court had venue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So we have document number 26 on the monitor which I requested to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, would you please read for us the heading on the first page of this document and its date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading, "Federal Secretariat for National Defence, administration for moral guidance, confidential number 6-83 of 12th October 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see page 2 of this document, please? And can we see the very bottom of the document, please? Mr. Djukic, who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go down to see paragraph -- scroll down, rather, to see the second-from-the-bottom paragraph, the penultimate paragraph which starts with the words, "In the course of," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Read that paragraph for us, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "In the course of the execution of these tasks, at all costs must be prevented any arbitrary behaviour, lack of discipline, leaving without permission from units, maltreating of citizens, irrespective of their ethnicity, in the area where the units are deployed, the looting and theft of property, and the enforcement of some sort of private laws."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this document the -- an excerpt from which you have just read, does it confirm what you said before?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does confirm that and I should also like to add there was in my zone the famous mausoleum of Ivan Mestrovic, a Yugoslav-oriented artist of high repute and of high value for Yugoslavia. He was a Croat and we all liked him, and loved him, and I ordered that this mausoleum be protected. I personally ordered and not a stone had been touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see Exhibit number 59? And this one is no longer necessary. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Djukic, please read out the heading on the first page of this document, the date and the title.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading, "Command on the 9th Corps, strictly confidential number 580-15 of the 20th of October 1991. Combatting crime in the zone of combat operations of the 9th Corps, to the command of the first Partizan Brigade of the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please read the introduction and the first paragraph of this document, if it -- yes. It can be scrolled up a bit, thank you. So the introduction and the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "With a view to preventing the unauthorised conduct and the pursuit of criminal actions, such as the looting of property and jeopardising the security of citizens by members of the armed forces in the zone of operations of the 9th Corps, I hereby order: 1, commands of JNA and TO units shall organise updated records of all the members of the units, including volunteers and members of the Territorial Defence of the individual places, and shall place all such armed units under the command of JNA units of regiment brigade rank in the zone of responsibility of the operation of such units. All members of armed units should be warned of the consequences of violent behaviour, arbitrary conduct, and the perpetration of criminal acts."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also please read the third paragraph under point 2, which starts with the words, "All commands of JNA units."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All commands of JNA units, Territorial Defence Staffs and town commands, shall undertake all measures to protect citizens and property this their respective zones of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now turn over to page 2 of this document, please? And please, Mr. Djukic, read items 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "4, criminal complaints shall be filed through the closest command of JNA units in accordance with the provisions of the law on criminal procedure in respect of all persons in relation of whom there exists reasonable doubt that they have committed a criminal offence. Along with the complaint, statements of witnesses should be submitted as well as other evidence on the criminal offence perpetrated."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And item 5?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "5: The perpetrators of criminal offences falling under the jurisdiction of the military court should be deprived of liberty and through the police of the commands of regiments-brigades of the JNA, escorted to the military police in Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this, document excerpts from which you have just read, also confirm your order and did you implement it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does and we did comply with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can we now see Exhibit number 49, please? Mr. Djukic, will you read the heading, the date, and the title on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "Command of the 9th Corps, strictly confidential number 625-2, 31st of October 1991, Knin. In parentheses, 1600 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the title?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command for the execution of an offensive operation on the city of Sibenik, operational number 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. "Excerpt for the staff of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see this document ever before?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 7 of this document? And in the English version it is page number 8. So page 7 and 8 in the English version. Please read the last two paragraphs under item 7.2?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last two paragraphs under item 7.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Since the witness just said he's not seen this document before and he's not testified about what's contained in this document, I'm not sure what the foundation is for having the witness now read parts of the document. It seems more like cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my distinguished colleague, the Prosecutor, is right, and I shall -- yes, refrain from -- I shall abandon this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see document number 27?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document number 27 or Exhibit number 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit number 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 2? Sorry, before that, would you read for us the heading on the first page of this document, its date, and its title.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading, "Federal Secretariat for National Defence, General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, first department or first administration, strictly confidential, number 2256-2 of the 10th of December 1991. Sent to the command of the 9th Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the title?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says, "Please find here with enclosed directive of the Federal Secretary for National Defence on the use of the armed forces in the forthcoming period."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go to page 3 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- just for foundation purposes, I wonder when he saw the document before? Was it at the time or was it two days ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I asked the witness whether he had had occasion to see this document earlier, I was referring to period of many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document sometime late 1991 when it reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I asked to see that we be shown page 3 of this document, which is page 4 in the English translation. Under item 6, you can -- yes, under item 6, would you read that, the second paragraph of it for us?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "Employ all measures to prevent looting and genocidal, in brackets, revanchist, conduct. To that end, establish the necessary control by the engagement of organs of the military police and the units designated for that purpose, as well as organs for criminal prosecution."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Does this document also confirm what you just told us a while ago?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And to summarise, what is -- what was the position of the Yugoslav People's Army towards the population and property in the area of operations? Did you comply in full with the orders, the content of which we have just been familiarised with?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all these orders, other instructions, information memorandums from the second department of the SSNO and the General Staff, which actually conveyed the provisions of the laws on the armed forces of the SFRY, we, all the commanders I'm talking about my unit as well as the other units, as far as I know, we all complied with the provisions of all these orders and employed every possible measure to prevent what might happen in war, aware of the fact that war is the ultimate state of anarchy and having that in mind we did everything in our power to prevent negative incidents from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djukic, you mentioned a while ago that there had been such negative practices and that the perpetrators of adverse incidents were sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about damage to places of worship in the zone of the 9th Corps? Were there such damages to religious buildings during the operations that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the operations of the JNA units, no place of worship was damaged. We had instructions that even if there was action or fire opened from a place of worship that we were not to use heavy weaponry. But I do know that in later times, several religious buildings were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether, and if so under what circumstances, was the Catholic church in Kijevo damaged, whether it was damaged and if so, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information who the perpetrators were in regard of that church but we received information that most probably the -- they were, had been extremists from the ranks of the Serb people who had mined the church and blown it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those people identified and tried at some later point? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that. I know that some steps had been taken and how far that had gone, I have no idea because at that time, that particular area was not under the zone of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can we now see Exhibit 106 on the monitor? Mr. Djukic, could you read the heading of the first page of this document, the date and the addressee?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read: "Command of the 9th Corps, confidential, number 19-1549, dated 4th of October 1991, at 1500 hours. To the General Staff of the armed forces of SFRY, operational centre, and the command of the military naval district-IKM." IKM was located at the island of Vis, and this is the forward command post on the island of Vis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see this document, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that we had officers on duty in the operational centre of the command, I knew of this document. It was the relevant period that we are discussing, October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read to us the first two paragraphs under item 1.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down? Oh, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "1, corps units, during battle for Kijevo, on the 26th of August 1991, were engaged in a battle lasting more -- several hours, to break through the village and effectuate the lifting of a blockade of separated or blockaded units in the area of Kosorska Greda and Jajce [phoen] Glavica near the village of Civljani. Strongest resistance of the National Guards Corps was offered from the local church, a Catholic church, whose belfry housed a machine-gun position and the reconnaissance of the command of the ZNG company, who was captured during the action. The church housed the 1st Platoon of ZNG, which used the doors, windows and the belfry to open fire at our unit. From the immediate vicinity of the church or the perimeter of the cemetery, which is adjacent to the church, other forces of the aforementioned company of ZNG acted against -- through -- from well-built ramparts, which were reinforced by concrete, concrete blocks, and that company was composed of the reserve forces of ZNG mobilised in the villages of Kasteli, near Split. Members of that unit used graves, in brackets, already prepared, and some graves contained mortal remains, for cover."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you read also the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Although from the region of the church and the monastery beyond it, we received very strong fire, the church and the cemetery were spared direct fire because we fired at -- in the vicinity of these facilities on the hills and this fire was for warning purposes."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you read the last paragraph on this page? "The goal of your action."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The goal of our action is not, nor will it ever be, to destroy, religious, sacral or other invaluable facilities, on condition that these are not used as fortifications to open fire from, and that has been a regular occurrence until now. Chief of Staff, Colonel Ratko Mladic, signed."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What does this document tell you regarding the Kijevo church?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confirms what I already said, that we -- even in the cases when fire was opened from religious buildings, we never used heavy weaponry, tanks or artillery, against them. We blocked this area, I remember we captured 60 members of the ZNG in the graves of that cemetery, within the church, in a canal below the church as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During combat activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Perovic, at page 55, line 16 up to line 19, does the witness understand that to mean that in those circumstances that he spoke of there, then it would mean that you could destroy the church or you could return fire there? I'm sorry, not that one. I referred you to the wrong lines. In respect of 22 to 25, "the goal of our acting is not nor will it ever be to destroy religious, sacral, or other invaluable facilities unconditioned at these are not used as fortifications to open fire from." Does it mean then that if they are used as fortification to open fire from, then you would be at liberty to destroy them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer this question, please, witness?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our basic commitment was not to act against religious facilities. From -- on a case by case basis the situation on the ground may have required different solutions, but as far as I'm concerned as a commander of my unit, I never allowed destruction of religious facilities or cultural facilities, buildings, because of our positive attitude towards the cultural heritage of the peoples of Yugoslavia and I wanted to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood Her Honour Nosworthy's question, the question was this: If a sacral building were to be converted into a machine-gun post, would it be a legitimate target for the military? Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be a legitimate target because it was used to fire against military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry [Microphone not activated] Thank you so much. Earlier when we talked about damage to religious buildings, the witness said he didn't know anything about the Catholic church in Kijevo, I didn't know who the perpetrators who -- were because it was not in the area of -- in the zone of his responsibility. Now he seems to be talking very authoritatively about this very damage to this very church, now that we are dealing with this topic. Is there an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, did you understand the -- His Honour, Judge Moloto's opinion?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have understood it. During the short term operation of lifting the blockade of the road through Kijevo, which is the site where this church is located, my orders stated that this facility must not be destroyed, and this was not done. It wasn't done on that day of our operation, the 26th of August 1991. That church, on that location, after the road was cleared, remained there until the unit was quartered there, and part of the unit was withdrawn from that direction pursuant to an order by the commander of the 9th Corps on the 23rd of September 1991. After that date, I cannot recall because I never visited that area, I found out that this church was destroyed subsequently. By the way, that church, that was built as an Orthodox church, it was orientated as an Orthodox church and it was used by the inhabitants of Kijevo who, pursuant to historical data, some 200 years ago, converted to Catholicism during the Austrian reign in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djukic, if I understood you correctly, you personally don't have much reliable information about the destruction of the Kijevo church?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's precisely my question. And now from this latest answer, I get another -- it further confused, because he says at line 23 it wasn't done on that day of our operation, the 26th of August 1991. Now, by that, I understand him to be saying that on the 26th of August 1991, they were in Kijevo, but previously he said Kijevo was not in his area of responsibility. That's the first question that I'd asked earlier. Secondly, the next part of my question is: If indeed he knew nothing about the destruction of the Kijevo Catholic church, how does he speak so authoritatively to this document that we have on the screen, which is talking about the destruction of the Catholic church in Kijevo? Those are my two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, did you understand this question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The first question would be within the area of your responsibility during the operation to lift the blockade of the Kijevo road, was this church within that area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That church is located in the village of Kijevo, and during this short lasting operation of the unit that I commanded, the operation to establish buffer zones and to clear the road, that church was not destroyed, and I prohibited, by an order, my order, to have this church targeted, although, as it's stated in this report, through my operational organ to the commander of the 9th Corps which was then later forwarded further, although fire was opened from that church. I remained on the axis which included Kijevo until the 23rd of October 1991. And up to that date, that church stood undestroyed, stood intact. How can I explain it to you? It was there. And on the 23rd of October 1991, I was ordered to withdraw my unit, one of the units that was on that axis, to perform other tasks, and I just explained that other task was to secure the withdrawal of JNA from Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me get this right. During your stay or your unit's stay in Kijevo, the church stood intact. My question --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was it damaged?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some windows were blown, and there were minor damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What caused that damage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe during the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we've reached a good time to take the break, unless you wish us to clarify further this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because fire was opened from the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. I've seen the report. It is just the authoritative way he was speaking to the report that was causing me concern. It still does because this document is a document of the 4th of October, and he passed through Kijevo on the 26th of August, and he hasn't testified to doing anything else in Kijevo specifically after the 26th of August. I understand that he says his unit withdrew on the 23rd of October, but without having done anything. So it is still a mystery to me how he speaks so authoritatively to this document. We take the break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. During the break, we translated item 11 that we mentioned and we made enough copies for the Chamber and our learned friends of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May Madam Usher distribute these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you, Honourable Judge Moloto have any questions with regards to what we discussed towards the end of the previous session, I mean the church in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, except the remark that I made, it's just an observation I made that he speaks quite authoritatively on this document when it seems from his evidence that what is mentioned in this document, he has no knowledge of. It's just an observation I'm making.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, I'd like to ask you this: During the carrying out of combat operations within the zone of responsibility of the 9th Corps, apart from JNA units, were there any other forces, if so, which forces?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area of responsibility, we had Territorial Defence units operating from municipalities which were included in the zone of the 9th Corps except for the municipality of Sinj, where no Territorial Defence units were engaged, and of course the municipalities of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What time are you referring to with this question? It's very important. The question which was just answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the second part of 1991 and the operations around Sibenik, Drnis, Kijevo, and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered that units of the Territorial Defence Staffs of the mentioned two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did these units operate autonomously or were they subordinated to any command? If so, whose command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence units did not operate autonomously. They were subordinated to commands depending on their location or depending on the axis of operations and combat activities. In principle, Territorial Defence detachments or battalions would be under a brigade, and Territorial Defence brigades were subordinated to the 9th Corps. This is a principle that was applied during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, those units of the Territorial Defence were subordinated to the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit 26 on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a communique from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. I believe it has been used already. We used it a while ago. Can we see page 2 of this document, please? Scroll up, please, so that we can see the last paragraph of this page. This is it. The last paragraph which starts with the words, "All armed units." Will you please read that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "All armed units, whether they be JNA, Territorial Defence, or volunteers, must operate under the single command of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient. What did this mean concretely when it came to their use?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that they cannot operate on their own, they had to be subordinated to the units and commands of the JNA. That was the principle and that was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the orders and the instructions of the JNA that we referred to a while ago, which regarded discipline and the treatment of the population and the property, did they also refer to those forces?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, in full, and everything was implemented as in relation to the units of the JNA, and they also belonged to military prosecutorial offices and military courts during the time of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If these forces were under JNA command, as you say, was the Yugoslav People's Army also responsible for their discipline too?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In a situation of a member of such forces committing a criminal offence while a member of and under the command of the JNA, who had jurisdiction for the prosecution and trials of such persons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military courts were -- had jurisdiction, and I can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not need this document any more and you can kindly take it off the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, we shall now move on to another topic. You were born in the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You hail from that republic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From a village in the vicinity of the former Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the village of Gornji Vodica. Now it is -- it used to be Bosanski Novi and now it is Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were you arrested in 1991, General? Where did this happen and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested by the paramilitary or parapolice forces of the time in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which having -- organised by the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were arrested and when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested in September, on the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother, my own brother, Dzemail had died. He was very young. He was 35. I received a cable and I asked my superior commanding officer to grant me a leave so that could go and attend my brother's funeral. I was given such permission, and he even recommended that I take a military vehicle and security guards with me. He wanted me to take those. I didn't do that. I just took a driver who was a reserve officer. He was a sergeant, and he was actually also a member of the SUP Knin, and in fact, he was the secretary of the SUP Knin. He came along with me. On the next morning, and I didn't watch the news, I came to -- so the next morning I came to the village of Otaci [phoen], which is near my village, and I found a huge crowd of people who had blocked the bridge from the village of Otoka towards the other end which is the village of Blatina and in the direction of Novi Grad. Halfway through the bridge, I was blocked by an infuriated throng of people. They hit the vehicle. They hit me. They beat up the driver. They inflicted grave injuries on me. I had two ribs broken and nicks and cuts on my hands. They even tried to throw me in the river. Later I was taken to -- in fact I'm not sure whether there is a police station in that village. I was taken to a room in which was the then Deputy Minister of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whom I recognised from having seen him on television, Avdo Hebib, a physician by profession otherwise. And I asked him how and why this has happened and he told me to wait, and I asked him to check things out. In the police station of Novi Grad, i.e., the former Bosanski Novi, from the Commander Haro, who used to go to school with me, I wanted to check with him whether my brother had really died and to let me go, to pass through. Anyway, while I was waiting there, they put me in a room in which was Mr. Mile Martic, with two of his escorts, and Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not quite catch the surname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was also there with a junior officer whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the surname of the person the interpreter didn't catch the name, the surname. Dusko's surname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dusko Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I got after being released, when I got home, using the telephone at my brother's house, I informed the command of the corps what had happened to me, and who was there arrested in the village of Ovtaci [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Were you wearing a uniform and was Lieutenant-Colonel Smiljanic wearing a uniform while you were on that trip?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all in uniform. Mr. Smiljanic, Colonel Smiljanic was and his escort was but I was in civilian clothes and my driver was in mufti too but in a military vehicle with JNA marks, licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you were then returned -- released after the interrogation, after one hour. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the people remained there in those premises where they had been arrested. I informed the corps command, and then measures followed, namely I have to say that when I arrived in my brother's apartment, I asked that one of the JNA units which was there be subordinated to me so that I could free two members of the Yugoslav People's Army, namely Lieutenant-Colonel Smiljanic and his escort, and it goes without saying that I would have also freed Mr. Martic on that occasion. This was not allowed to me to do. They said that certain measures would be taken and I learned during the day that they had been freed, and another thing which happened was that people on learning about this started to spontaneously assemble, the people from the surrounding area of the villages. It was not a state of war so people wielding hunting rifles headed towards Otaci to liberate these two JNA members and Mr. Martic, then the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. So on that occasion, the occasion which you're describing, four members of the Yugoslav People's Army had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is September 1991 that we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did at that time -- was at that time this republic a part of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, this republic absolutely was a part of the SFRY, and in that republic at that time, no major incidents happened, even though there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you something about an operation called Corridor 92. Were you a participant in the operation of a break through or through the Corridor 92?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me according to whose decision and in what capacity did you participate in that operation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in that operation on my own. It was my own decision. I participated as a volunteer. That was the case with me as well as with all the members of the Territorial Defence of then at the time of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, special police units and the police of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What circumstances made it necessary to conduct this operation called Corridor 92?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the basic estimation, assessment of the situation, the circumstances that obtained were as follows: Croatia and its leadership had accepted the peacekeeping forces of the United Nations. At that time, they did not -- it did not have sufficient troops, armed forces, to integrate the Republic of Serbian Krajina into its republic by force. I mentioned that the review of the National Guards Corps was carried out in Zagreb at Jarun on the 28th of May 1991, and that at that time, they only had four regular brigades of the SZNG, the 1st and 2nd Zagreb Brigade, the 3rd Osijek Brigade, and the 4th Split Brigade. Normally these forces grew and swelled and according to information of the Main Staff of the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina towards the end of 1993, they numbered about 150.000 and just prior to the Storm Operation, about 200.000 members. At that time, the basic strategy of Croatia was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you slow down a little bit? It looks like the interpreter is struggling to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At that time, the Croatian leadership adopted an extremely perfidious and cunning strategy that to shift combat operations from its territory to another territory and they shifted them to the territory of the then Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1992 period, namely the period immediately after the start of the deployment of the UN forces, i.e., when the Vance Plan became operational, which was in January 1991 and already in February 1992, we have enormous Croatian forces in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to the available data at that time prior to the corridor operation, from Croatia were sent between 21 to 22 brigades to Bosnia and Herzegovina, a total of 35.000 to 40.000 members, which number at a certain point in 1992 even swelled to 50.000. All these figures have been confirmed, and this means that more than a third of the effective part of the armed forces of Croatia were engaged on the territory of another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what was the objective of the establishment of this corridor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me just one sentence by the -- this blockade in alliance with the forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia cut off the main road somewhere in the area of Doboj which is some halfway between the territory of Croatia from the west to the east, and in this way, it encircled 2000 -- 2 million, sorry, inhabitants. About 400.000 in the Serbian Krajina, and about 1 million and 500.000 in the ARK which is in the Bosnian Krajina in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in other words. The objective was, by this economic blockade when there was a humanitarian disaster practically speaking, there was no fuel, there was no other sources of energy, there were no medicaments, there was no food, the Red Cross was unable to deliver the necessary foodstuffs, humanitarian organisations were unable to operate, all flights had been forbidden by the United Nations Security Council. We had therefore a very difficult humanitarian situation and, by way of example, in the clinic in Banja Luka, 12 babies died in just one day, and let me tell you two months ago, the 13th of that -- those babies died, and she got sick for lack of oxygen and she was buried in Prijedor. So this strategy and economic pressure and this blockade was intended to integrate the Republic of Serbian Krajina into the Republic of Croatia by force, i.e., to have the other side, Alija Izetbegovic, the President of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to also subjugate a wide area containing some 1.500.000 Serbs in the autonomous Republic of Krajina in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, please try to be as concise and concrete as possible. So the goal of this operation, as I understood and correct me if I'm wrong, was to prevent a humanitarian disaster from happening. Did I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of the operation carried out by the forces of the army of the Republika Srpska was to prevent a humanitarian disaster from happening. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any other goal that you may know of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any other goals to establish land link with the Yugoslavia and the eastern part of Republic of Serbian Krajina, Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why this land link necessary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the functioning of our authorities and apart from that, the eastern part of the RSK was quite well -- rich and the western part of the RSK which was very poor, depended on the eastern part and of course from Serbia we provided -- had provisions of agricultural produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does a corridor between the RSK and Serbia facilitate communication between the eastern part of the RSK with the western part of the RSK? I don't understand how that happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? The eastern and western parts of the RSK did not have -- did not border. The Republic of Serbian Krajina was composed of two parts, and those two parts were divided by Bosnia-Herzegovina and part of Serbia which is called Vojvodina. To the north of that was Croatia and we could not communicate through Croatia. This was the territory under the control of the then Croatian authorities, and there was no land communication with that part. It functioned this way. It was strange, but it functioned. It worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we may show this on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the atlas, page 13, Exhibit 23. On this map, I believe it would be best seen and shown by the witness to mark out the western part and the eastern part of the RSK. We should move to the left, please. I believe this is fine. I propose that the witness mark with a pencil the boundaries of the western and the eastern parts of the RSK and maybe indicate the route of the corridor on this map by the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just saying thank you to Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be brought down a bit for the map to show Beli Manastir. Slightly to the left, please. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the boundaries of the eastern part?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I'm doing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the border towards Serbian Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is seen. It is concurrent with the river Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to roughly indicate the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see where the witness is drawing. My map is -- well, it's disappeared now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, this seems to be a little unclear now. Weren't we going to see the eastern part of the RSK and the western part of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right. What the witness is encircling is the eastern part of the RSK, Slavonia, and Baranja. The western part cannot be seen. We should move the map to the left, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, let the witness tell us what he's doing rather than you telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you have encircled a place there. I can't see the names but any way, it encloses Vukovar, it comes into Vinkovci, it encompasses, Osijek, goes right up. What is all that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, it doesn't encompass Vinkovci and it doesn't encompass Osijek. They are all left out of the boundaries. Includes this part, the villages between Otoka and Dimijenci [phoen]. This would be the area known as Western Srem. This is Eastern Slavonia what I'm showing now and up north it's the Baranja region. So there were three districts. This would be the border. Eastern part of the RSK, Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was completely separate from the western part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... me, because I don't follow what you say unless I understand what you have said. You said, "This is the boundary," and I don't see where you're pointing. Bear my question in mind. All I want you to show us is Eastern RSK, Western RSK, and the corridor to Serbia. That's what I want to see. And I want to see -- understand how the corridor to Serbia facilitates communication between the rich east of RSK and the poor west of RSK. That's what I want to understand. Show us Western RSK and then show us Eastern RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just drawn the boundaries of the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And this region was officially called Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as a district. These would be the boundaries, and it borders Serbia or the part of Serbia called Vojvodina to the east and to the west, we have the boundaries or the city limits and municipal limits of Osijek and Vinkovci. Vojvodina is to the east. This is wartime, showing Subotica, Backa Palanka, Vrbas. These are -- this is an autonomous province within Serbia. It's northern province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is Western RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to move the map so I can indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We have to save it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have to ascertain something before we save it. Are you saying that the whole of the line, the delineation line, is what would constitute Eastern RSK? Because it seems to be split into two parts to me, an upper part and lower part. Is it -- well, Judge Moloto is saying three. I thank him for pointing out to me. I hadn't even noticed that. Are you saying, then, Witness -- thank you, Judge -- that all three that are delineated would have constituted Eastern RSK, the whole of that is Eastern RSK, including Eastern Slavonia and the Baranja region and the other region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've just drawn here is part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We can call it the eastern part of the RSK which had the name. This is one district, and had it a single name, which was Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem so there are three entities within it, eastern Slavonia is in the middle, Baranja is north, where Beli Manastir is, that's Baranja, and to the south is Western Srem. So what I indicated here on the map is an integral part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina but is physically disconnected from the western part of the RSK which I'm about to show you and indicate on the map in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. The part right at the bottom, at the south, would then be Western Srem? And in the middle would be Baranja or am I misunderstanding it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in the middle would be Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So what would be at the top, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Baranja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And do we understand you correctly, Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and the very southern one is Western Srem, together would constitute one province or one district, the district of eastern RSK, or is that right, eastern part of RSK? Or are these three municipalities or what is the political structure of these three pieces and of the one piece consisting of the three ones? Just in one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were more municipalities, Beli Manastir, Darda [phoen], Vukovar, Tenja, these were municipalities of Ilok, these were municipalities located in that area, and that area had several municipalities but they directly border Republic of Serbian Krajina, were part of it. They were connected with Knin which is located in the western portion, so to speak, of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, this we will see now but just before we see that we wanted to have clarification on the meaning of this three parts of eastern part of RSK. Just to finish that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is part of the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Djukic, that the western part of the RSK is not -- I thought I understood you to say is not contiguous to the eastern part. It's separated by something else. What is in between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see, when I draw it, sir, a large portion of the Republic of Croatia and a large portion of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The western part of the RSK is quite a long way away from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you saying that the eastern part -- this eastern region, eastern part of the RSK is contiguous somehow to Serbia? Vojvodina, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The border is the river Danube. You can see on the Hungarian border the village of Baja. This constitutes a border, the red line indicates the border between the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Croatia. At that time it was part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The districts of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem. Or Eastern Srem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is it Western Srem or Eastern Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eastern Srem because it's in the east. The west is in the opposite direction. I correct myself. Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for this intervention, I'm just thinking aloud. Would it be easier for the Chamber for this map to be placed on the ELMO so that the Chamber may follow which parts are being indicated by the General? He's indicating and pointing at the screen, which you cannot see. It would be much more worthwhile for that to place -- to be placed on the ELMO so that you can follow the indications, the places pointed out by the General. I believe that this would be more useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm -- you failed to switch your microphone on so I couldn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to know whether you endorse what Mr. Milovancevic is saying because you are the one now in control of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it would be helpful to you, I am in full agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it possible to put it on the ELMO? If it's at all possible to have both eastern and western on the ELMO at the same time, it would be very helpful, and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What page of the atlas is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 13, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It's so small.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see well. Your Honours, I have the original map of the Republic of Serbian Krajina where you can see everything very nicely. So with your permission, may I show it to you? And can I explain things to you using that map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Will you have a copy of the map at the same time or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This map is in evidence in our case. I don't recall what the number is, it may be a little investigating and in fact I've never seen an original because if you recall this is the map that has the writing on the back. We have the translation. So I'm quite grateful to see an original of it. But I'm happy to proceed with this map. We do have a map book and there is a good map which shows this quite clearly. It's Exhibit 22, I believe, page 7. I think that that would -- it's actually even clearer but however the Defence wants to proceed I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're happy with that, Mr. Perovic, that map? Mr. Perovic, are you happy with the use of that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm happy with any proposal which will help us clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Black, the ever-helpful Mr. Black, tells me that it's Exhibit 3 in evidence, this map, and I believe there is a translation of the back but that's not really relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. And thank you very much to Mr. Black, too. Now, okay. Are we going -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Allow me to explain. Here on the map you can see, this is the east part. To the east, what I'm showing now is Serbia, i.e., its northern province of Vojvodina. As I go west, that is the Republic of Croatia, this border here, and to the south, that is Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this here, that is the western part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, and you can see that it is physically separated from the east part. From here, a land link could not be established because this was the Republic of Croatia with their authority, army and police, but we had to establish a link via the direction of Banja Luka, which we do not see now here, but that is the corridor route which breaks out into two crossings, Pavlovica Most and Raca into the Republic of Serbia from which crossings then you go up to this part. So it goes through Bosnia and Herzegovina into Serbia and then up to this part of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll still put my question because that's how I thought I heard you when you testified, that you were saying, and do correct me if I misheard you. I understood you to say that you were establishing a corridor between the eastern part of the RSK, which is rich, and Serbia so that you should be able to help the poorer western part. Hence my question was: How does connecting eastern RSK with Serbia help the poor western RSK? And now that there is actually some other land in between the two RSKs, my question becomes even more pertinent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The west part of the RSK, the only life line for it was this corridor called the Operation Corridor, which went through Bosnia and Herzegovina and from Bosnia and Herzegovina into Serbia, through Serbia up to the east part of the RSK, this part. And the only link was a land link. So these parts could be connected via Banja Luka and Doboj and one could enter Serbia at two points, namely at the crossing of Raca and the Pavlovica Cuprija, meaning Pavlovica bridge, point which are not marked because we don't see that part of Serbia because it is more to the south. So we had to establish a link through Bosnia and Herzegovina, and through a part of Serbia to reach the east part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in order to connect its western part, so to connect the western part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina with its eastern part we had to pass through two other republics. I hope that I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that you are pointing to the map it's clearer. In fact, the corridor starts from the western part of RSK, it doesn't start from the east, which is how you -- that's how you came up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how it came up on the screen but I understand you now, sir. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you're one of the immediate participants in the events that we talked about today and yesterday. According to your knowledge, who is the -- who committed a criminal enterprise in that period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to everything that one experienced and everything that transpired practically on the ground, it is evident that the Republic of Croatia, with its army, as a state, namely the Republic of Croatia, committed the criminal enterprise against the Serbian people in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and against the Serbian people in the territory of the Republika Srpska, that is to say a part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djukic, this concludes my examination-in-chief of you as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Djukic, my name is Alex Whiting and I'm one of the prosecutors in this case. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, before I ask you any questions, I want to ask you, please, if you would, listen to my questions very carefully and just answer my questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Most of the time you'll be able to just say you agree or disagree. Long explanations will not be necessary, okay?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, before we get into the topics, I do want to ask you a question about your memory about -- with respect to time because it is after all we are talking about events that occurred 15, 14, 13 years ago. Do you have a sense that you have a good memory for the time, the time that events occurred in 1990, 1991, or is your memory about time not necessarily so clear?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I retired in 1994, I put down on paper, making notes on everything that had happened, and I published one book, I had one book published, and work on the publishing of another two is underway and with a colleague of mine, a subordinated officer of mine, I prepared another book which is soon to come out of print so that I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you and I don't do that disrespectfully it's only because you've now said several sentences but you haven't answered my question. If you could really just answer the question: How is your memory concerning time from that period? Do you have a good memory or not a good memory?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have a very good memory, especially for some things which impressed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at Exhibit 458, please? And if we could look -- right, keep moving, keep moving, perfect. Do you see that photograph? It's a photograph of four men, there are two photographs on this page and the photograph I want to focus on is the one on left that has four men on it. Do you see that photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise from the left to the right, Mile Paspalj, president of the assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, next to him in uniform, I myself. And next to me, Mr. Mile Martic, in police uniform. And at the right end, the commander of the Serbian army of the Krajina, General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this photograph, but I suppose that it was perhaps after the Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That would be what dates, please? After the Operation Corridor would be after what date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded the operation on the 17th of July 1992, and returned to Knin on the 17th of July 1992, so it is perhaps about that time. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise the background, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you don't remember the occasion that this photograph -- you don't remember the occasion when the four of you were together like this after the corridor operation and a photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a minor thing. It is us on the photograph and it's from about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you don't remember, it's fine. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was made general after the Operation Corridor so that this photograph dates to that time, after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there some -- is there something that indicates to you from this photograph that you are a general?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said I am a general and was promoted to general on the 18th of July 1992, so that this photograph was taken after Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm just asking if there is something about the uniform you're wearing or any insignia which indicates that you're a general in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doesn't look like you understand the question, Mr. Djukic. The question is: Is there anything on this photograph that distinguishes you as a general? Is there anything in your uniform here that says, "This is something that is worn by a general"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see the emblem of a general, the patch on the left pocket of my blouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And thank you, sir. Now, the uniform you're wearing is the uniform of what exactly? Of what entity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the official uniform of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, but this is a uniform which I wore as the commander of the special police units, i.e., the head of the administration of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that function was within the Ministry of the Interior, wasn't it, sir? Not within the army.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That function was -- had a dual connection. Along one line, it was connected to the Ministry of Defence and along the other to the Ministry of the Interior. The professional part of the execution of the task was connected to the Ministry of the Interior, and I was in my capacity of head of that administration, one of the assistants to the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That we'll talk about more later, but just to be clear the uniform that you're wearing and that Mr. Novakovic is wearing, those are uniforms of the RSK army, correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain period, because of securing the borders, the police uniforms were changed and were no longer blue but were camouflage uniforms as the one that you can see me wearing as Western Srem as General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying that that is a police uniform that you're wearing? You and Mr. Novakovic are wearing police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the police units, at a certain period, in a certain period, especially those units which were on the border, they wore these camouflage, motley uniforms, the police did. You can see the combination. I have blue trousers and camouflage blouse and a Blue Beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The uniform you're wearing is different from the uniform that Mr. Novakovic is wearing, correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm looking at it on this photo, it differs, we had different uniforms for the same posts in the same units. We had different nuances of uniforms procured from different manufacturers, even the colouring of the blouses and the trousers were not the same. These differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When I asked to you identify the people in this photograph, you identified the man on the right-hand side as the commander of the Serbian army of the Krajina, General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and he was the commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina, appointed at the end of November, all the way to 1994. I don't know, February or March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what is he in this photograph? You were talking about the photograph when you said it but now are you telling us that he had a different function in this -- when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. In accordance with the emblem that he's I see that we are wearing the same emblem. We wear similar uniforms but I cannot provide you with a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But am I right in saying that you told us a little earlier that the uniform you are wearing is the one you wore as the commander of the special police units, not the army? You said that at page 84, line 7 to 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never an army commander. I commanded a brigade within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question. I never said you were an army commander. I said, am I right in saying that you have told us a couple of minutes ago that the uniform you are wearing is the one which you wore as the commander of the special police units? You can say yes, you are right, or no, you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume that this photograph was taken while I was the commander of the special units of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: The uniform you are wearing is the uniform you wore in your capacity as a commander of the special police units? Am I right in saying so? Or were you misinterpreted here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is the uniform that I wore, that I wore in my capacity as commander of the special units of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. And this general on the right, you say, at this time, he was wearing a uniform of the army, RSK army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot narrow down to the very date. That general was subordinated to me while I was commander of the special units of police. He was a commander of one of the brigades in the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I'm not asking you about dates or time. I'm just asking you, this general is wearing a uniform of the army, not of the special police units. That's in your evidence a little earlier. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wears a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, please, I'm just asking you a simple question. Is this the uniform of the police, army of the RSK, or is it not? You know there are various military uniforms here and we can see that there are different uniforms. We want to identify which one belongs to which. Please be cooperative. You've told us yours is of the police -- special police units. What does this one, this other uniform belong to? You said it is the army. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my uniform could be a military uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. That's not part of the question that I asked. You've answered my questions. Thank you very much. I'm sorry it's taken me so long to get that clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you're not able to tell us what the function of General Novakovic was at that time, when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall this detail. Judging from this picture, I could pinpoint the date whether it was taken, maybe, but I don't have this photo. If I were to have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry but you told us earlier that this photograph was taken, I believe you said, after the 18th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the 17th of July 1992. Are you having difficulty telling us what General Novakovic's position was after that date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Novakovic, after the 18th of July 1992, up until the end of November 1992, was the commander of a brigade of special units of police for the Kordun district. He was subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why is he wearing a different uniform?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we procured uniforms from different manufacturers. We differed in shades of the uniforms, not by the type. This is a camouflage fatigues on both of us, but they are different shading. They are slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why, when you identified him in the photograph, did you identify him as a general in the army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a general of the Serbian Army of Krajina, commander of the chief -- General Staff of the SVK, and he held that position from the end of November up until the appointment of the new general, General Celeketic, which took place at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Appointment of the new commander, General Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We have got to take a break and come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this Court. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
